html_en:
The AI industry is sorting itself into winners and losers faster than most people realize — and today's conversation makes clear that the deciding factor won't be who has the most capital, but who has the sharpest insight.

🏗️ The Architecture of Efficient Agents

The most practically important idea circulating today comes from Cursor's new research, surfaced by Box CEO Aaron Levie: frontier models as planners, cheaper models as workhorses — and the result is a 15x cost improvement on complex coding tasks.

"Few moments in a large task genuinely require frontier intelligence, such as the original decomposition, the design decisions, and certain trade-offs. Once a frontier planner has collapsed the ambiguity into a detailed, explicit instruction, less expensive models simply have to follow it." — @levie, quoting Cursor's research

Levie's framing is sharp: this tiered routing approach is "increasingly becoming the core design pattern of complex agents," and the companies that master it — across coding, legal, finance, healthcare — will be able to take on workloads that would otherwise be economically unviable for customers to deploy.

The agent design conversation also surfaced a neat practical problem: self-preferential bias. @trq212, speaking on a recent podcast episode, explained the fix:

"For something like, 'Is this a good video short or not?' you don't have a deterministic answer. You should have a separate verification agent read a rubric, review the short, and give feedback. We call it self-preferential bias. When a model prefers its own output, it's going to be more lenient at verifying it." — @trq212, via @petergyang

Watch/Listen: Full episode linked by @petergyang

🔬 Benchmark Laundering and the Hidden Trajectory Problem

A more uncomfortable conversation is brewing around AI model evaluation. @swyx flagged a notable section buried in a new Reinforcement Learning Models (RLM) paper from @a1zhang and @lateinteraction that puts a name to something many insiders already suspect:

"An open secret of 'frontier' model training is that even without training on test, you can basically cheat by training on test lookalikes, enabling you to goalseek almost any benchmark number you want. However when they are released open weights, 99% of the time the norm is that you do not get the datasets/rlenvs that would easily show you if someone was training on Temu Tbench, so there is plausible deniability." — @swyx

The paper proposes applying standard NLP distance metrics to hidden model trajectories as a preliminary probe. It's not a silver bullet, but it's a start — and the findings also support a more encouraging conclusion: that RLMs can genuinely generalize to unseen tasks sharing latent structure with their training distribution. The cheating problem and the generalization question, it turns out, are two sides of the same coin.

💡 "Everything Is Code" — And Other Paradigm Shifts

Few tweets this week landed harder than this one from Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch, which accumulated over 4,300 likes:

"The big lesson from AI is that everything is code. A slide deck is code. Design is code. That cool promo video? Code. Excel automation? Code. The universe? Probably made of code too." — @rauchg

It sounds glib, but it captures something real about the current moment: the surface area of what's programmable — and therefore automatable — is expanding rapidly. Replit CEO Amjad Masad pushed this further, teasing what may be the first physical product shipped by a coding agent — a provocation worth watching.

Meanwhile, @zarazhangrui offered the clearest organizational lens on what this shift means for companies:

"There are basically two kinds of companies now. The ones built before coding agents showed up, scrambling to retrofit. And the ones founded after. The second type is different from day one: teams under ten people because they actually don't need more. Work organized by projects, not departments. Each person closes their own loop. Almost no internal meetings." — @zarazhangrui

🏆 Capital Is Not a Moat

The day's most important cautionary note came from @nikunj, whose historical analogy deserves wide circulation among founders currently flush with AI investment:

"Many founders in the last 18 months are going to realize that just because there are no 'moats' in AI left anymore doesn't mean 'scale and capital' become your main moat... Each one [Webvan, Groupon, MySpace, Yahoo, Blockbuster, Nokia] was structurally and capital-wise in a very good position, but eventually got beat by a company with a much better unique insight. Or just collapsed under the weight of their own scale." — @nikunj

This rhymes with what Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel told the No Priors podcast — a man who has watched a $30 billion market cap collapse to a few hundred million and then climb back to $180 billion over 27 years:

"There is no such thing as a moat. There is no such thing as somewhere you're gonna be protected against innovation. Today, we have a competitive advantage on areas. Absolutely. But those can go away tomorrow. The only one to win long term is to continue to develop new services, new ways to do things." — Glenn Fogel, No Priors

Watch/Listen: Travel Through the Lens of AI with Booking.com CEO Glenn Fogel — No Priors

Separately, @petergyang made a pointed geopolitical observation that fits this same frame: "Banning Chinese models will be the same self own as banning Chinese EVs." Protectionism, history suggests, rarely substitutes for building something genuinely better.

🎭 The Hiring Test Is Being Rewritten

Finally, a practical note on talent. @zarazhangrui proposed a two-round interview structure that is quietly becoming the template for AI-native companies:

"Round 1: in-person & no AI allowed; test domain expertise and knowledge on the fly. Round 2: a project that must be done with AI (impossible to complete without AI). Candidate assessed not just on the result but also the chat transcript with agents." — @zarazhangrui

The chat transcript detail is the key innovation here. How someone prompts and iterates with an agent is increasingly the job — and it's finally becoming legible as an evaluable skill.
html_zh:
今天的AI圈围绕着一个核心矛盾展开：模型越来越强大，但评估它们的方式正在失效——与此同时，"万物皆代码"的浪潮正在重塑企业组织的基本逻辑。

🔬 基准测试的黑暗面：有人在作弊吗？

AI圈长期存在一个公开的秘密，这周终于有人系统性地捅破了它。@swyx 在推特上指出了一篇被埋藏在RLM论文中的重要分析：

"'前沿'模型训练的公开秘密是：即使不直接在测试集上训练，也可以通过训练'测试题长相似'的数据来作弊，从而几乎可以让任何基准分数随心所欲。然而当开放权重模型发布时，99%的情况下你拿不到训练数据集或强化学习环境，所以作弊者有充分的合理推诿空间。"
— @swyx

论文作者 @a1zhang 和 @lateinteraction 尝试用标准NLP距离指标分析隐藏的推理轨迹，探索是否能识别"训练了测试题近似版"的模型。虽然没有终极解法，但初步探索令人警醒——同时也支持了一个积极发现：真正泛化能力强的RLM，确实能迁移到训练中未见过、但共享潜在结构的任务上。

🤖 智能体架构的新范式：用前沿模型规划，用廉价模型执行

本周最值得收藏的产品洞见，来自 Box CEO Aaron Levie 对Cursor最新研究的解读。核心结论：在复杂任务中，并非每一步都需要顶级智能。

"大型任务中真正需要前沿智能的时刻寥寥无几——比如最初的任务分解、关键设计决策，以及某些权衡取舍。一旦前沿规划者将模糊性压缩成详细、明确的指令，廉价模型只需照章执行即可。"
— @levie 引用Cursor研究

Levie指出，这种"前沿模型当指挥，廉价模型干苦力"的架构，可以带来15倍的成本降低。谁能在垂直领域（法律、医疗、金融）掌握这套路由逻辑，谁就能拿下原本"太贵用不起"的大规模工作负载。

与此呼应，@petergyang 分享了一个视频制作领域的具体案例。@trq212 解释了为什么验证不能交给生产内容的同一个模型：

"我们称之为自我偏好偏差（self-preferential bias）。当模型偏爱自己的输出时，它在验证时会更宽松。"
— @petergyang 转述 @trq212

Watch/Listen: No Priors — Travel Through the Lens of AI with Booking.com CEO Glenn Fogel

💡 万物皆代码：一个新世界观正在成形

本周传播最广的一句话，来自 Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch，简洁到有些令人眩晕：

"AI带来的最大启示是：万物皆代码。PPT是代码。设计是代码。那个酷炫的宣传视频？代码。Excel自动化？代码。宇宙？大概也是代码。"
— @rauchg（获得4300个赞）

这不仅仅是一句俏皮话。Replit CEO Amjad Masad 更进一步，展示了据称是编程智能体发货的第一件实体产品——代码正在突破屏幕的边界。

与此同时，@zarazhangrui 观察到企业组织正在发生的结构性分裂：

"现在基本上有两种公司。一种是在编程智能体出现之前建立的，正在忙着改造自己；另一种是之后创立的，从第一天起就不一样：团队不超过十人，因为他们真的不需要更多；工作按项目而非部门组织；每个人自己闭环；几乎没有内部会议。"
— @zarazhangrui

🌏 地缘政治与开源：禁止中国模型是在搬石头砸自己的脚？

@petergyang 抛出了这周最具争议的政策判断：

"禁止中国模型，将和禁止中国电动车一样是一次自我伤害。"
— @petergyang（获得1000+赞）

@mattturck 则用一张表情包调侃OpenAI和Anthropic在免费中国开源模型发布时的反应，语气轻松，但背后的竞争焦虑是真实的。@realmadhuguru 也指出，今天真正重要的"代币经济学"辩论，早已不是web3时代的那些，而是开放权重 vs 闭源、推理成本与模型路由。

📋 创业与招聘：规模不是护城河，洞见才是

Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel在 No Priors 播客中的一句话，与当下的AI创业热潮形成了微妙共鸣：

"护城河并不存在。没有任何地方能让你永久免受创新冲击……如果你认为自己能轻松击败这些大玩家，我建议你在押注资本之前，先真正搞懂这门生意。"
— Glenn Fogel，No Priors

投资人 @nikunj 的警告同样值得所有创始人贴在墙上：Webvan、Groupon、MySpace……每一个都曾在结构和资本上占据优势，却最终败给了"拥有更好独特洞见"的对手，或者压垮于自身规模的重量。"找到值得十年以上坚持的独特洞见，同时足够审慎，不让资本和规模成为洞见的替代品"——这才是当下创始人需要穿针引线的地方。

招聘市场也在微妙变化：@nikunj 注意到，越来越多VC人才正在涌向快速成长的初创公司，头衔清一色是"Special Projects ⚡️"——颇像2012年的IB/咨询师转型潮。@zarazhangrui 则提出了一套新的面试框架：第一轮禁止AI，测试真实领域知识；第二轮必须用AI完成，还要提交与智能体的完整对话记录。
